papers.title: Ancestral sequence reconstruction enables functional expression of archaeal thermostable tungsten-containing aldehyde:ferredoxin oxidoreductases in E. coli
papers.abstract: Tungsten-containing enzymes offer important opportunities in industrial biocatalysis, e.g. to convert carboxylic acids into aldehydes without requiring co-substrates ATP and NADPH. These W-enzymes operate at low reduction potentials compared to the more ubiquitous Mo-enzymes, enabling unique reactions. Their application is limited by the lack of functional expression in commonly used heterologous host organisms. Here, we show that variants of Pyrococcus furiosus aldehyde:ferredoxin oxidoreductase (PfAOR) obtained using ancestral sequence reconstruction can be functionally expressed in E. coli with an activity of 0.86 U/mg towards crotonaldehyde at 60 {degrees}C, which is a 50-fold higher activity compared to the recombinant extant enzyme. The ancestral enzymes, named ThermoAOR3 and ThermoAOR4, carrying 61 and 84 mutations respectively, were purified using a single-step affinity purification, showed a kcat of 0.95 and 0.86 s-1 at 60 {degrees}C, respectively, and have Km values comparable to native PfAOR. ThermoAOR3 contained a redox active [4Fe-4S] cluster like native PfAOR. Furthermore, it contained 10-15% of the expected pterin cofactor, W and Fe, which indicates the enzyme production can still be improved. Altogether, we demonstrate the first heterologous expression of a functionally active W-AOR using a widely used bacterial host, which represents a breakthrough enabling exploration of these enzymes for industrial biocatalysis.

papers.title: Bivalent, Copper-Mediated Amyloid-β Binding Disruptsthe Prion Protein's Neuroprotective Conformation
papers.abstract: Emerging evidence shows that the cellular prion protein (PrPC) is a major receptor for Amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}) and that this aberrant interaction may influence the progression of Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, the molecular basis of this interaction remains poorly understood. Both proteins strongly bind Cu2+, and we previously discovered that PrPC, A{beta}30, and Cu2+ form a ternary complex at equimolar ratios. Here, using electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy with isotopically labeled proteins, we characterize the stoichiometry, stability, and molecular interactions of this ternary complex. We show that the complex forms preferentially at substoichiometric to equimolar Cu2+ concentrations yet remains stable at high Cu2+ ratios. The formation of the ternary complex is bivalent, requiring the previously identified A{beta}-binding domain on PrPC (residues 95-110) along with mutual Cu2+ coordination to the N-terminal octapeptide repeat domain in PrPC. Line broadening observed in A{beta}30 NMR experiments identifies its negatively charged N-terminal residues and central hydrophobic core (residues 17-21) as the primary PrPC binding sites. Through histidine mutation studies, we determine A{beta}30 coordinates Cu2+ primarily through His14. Critically, the ternary complex formation displaces Cu2+ from a specific His residue on the C-terminal domain of PrPC, disrupting the neuroprotective cis interdomain interaction that otherwise regulates the toxic effector N-terminal domain. Using segmentally isotopically 15N-labeled PrPC, we show that while the cis interaction is not fully eliminated by interaction with A{beta}, it becomes a disfavored conformational state. Together, these findings demonstrate how Cu2+ reinforces the PrPC-A{beta} interaction, in turn destabilizing PrPC's neuroprotective fold, offering a molecular mechanism for A{beta} accumulation at - and potential trafficking across - the plasma membrane.

papers.title: Sterically Controlled Conformational Gating of Rhodamine Spirolactam Switches for Super-Resolution Imaging
papers.abstract: The reversible interconversion of rhodamines between nonfluorescent spirocyclic and fluorescent ring-open states underpins fluorogenic probes and spontaneously blinking dyes for super-resolution imaging. Existing strategies mainly tune the equilibrium between these states through electronic modification, whereas the role of conformational return in ring closure remains less explored. Here, we establish steric regulation of rhodamine spirolactams through amide N-substituents. Bulky substituents generate intramolecular repulsion with the xanthene scaffold, favoring ring opening. Crystallographic observations reveal substantial amide reorientation upon opening, suggesting increased separation between the nitrogen and meso-carbon reaction centers. We propose that substituent-dependent conformational accessibility modulates C-N bond reformation and the lifetime of the emissive state. The tert-butyl-substituted dye 1e exhibits an open-state residence time of 145 ms, despite its lower pKcycl. Calculations also indicate a lower ring-opening barrier for 1e than for less hindered 1a (1.12 vs 1.37 eV). Incorporating this design into HaloTag probes enables SIM, STED, and SMLM imaging. Importantly, N-halo-RBRB enables dual-modal SIM/SMLM imaging with a single fluorophore, integrating the rapid reconstruction of overall cellular architecture by SIM with single-molecule localization information from SMLM. This work identifies sterically modulated conformational accessibility as a design principle for engineering reversible rhodamine switches with tailored imaging capabilities.

papers.title: Workflow for Assessing Mass Spectrometer Performance in Shotgun Lipidomics
papers.abstract: Reproducible and testable analytical performance of mass spectrometers is critical for inter-laboratory concordance of quantitative lipidomics analyses. However, common instrument readout or analyses of arbitrarily chosen lipid mixtures do not lend themselves to direct comparison between instruments independently configured and operated in different laboratories under in-house settings. We developed and validated the QC Shotgun workflow and web-accessible software that enable rapid testing, evaluation, documentation, and longitudinal monitoring of the performance of high-resolution mass spectrometers in quantitative shotgun lipidomics. Completed in less than 5 minutes, the QC Shotgun test reports 8 relative metric indices that facilitate inter-laboratory comparison and longitudinal assessment of instrument performance and identify deficiencies that are not apparent from instrument readouts. Systematic documentation of instrument status can improve inter-laboratory consistency and interpretation confidence of lipidomics datasets.

papers.title: De Novo Design of Miniprotein Binders Targeting the Leptin-Binding Site of the Leptin Receptor
papers.abstract: The leptin receptor (LEPR) regulates appetite, energy balance, glucose homeostasis, and neuroendocrine function and is closely associated with obesity, diabetes, and neurological disorders. Activation of LEPR signaling suppresses appetite and promotes energy expenditure, whereas impaired LEPR signaling and leptin resistance are commonly associated with obesity. Accordingly, modulation of LEPR signaling is a potential therapeutic strategy for obesity and related metabolic disorders. In this study, we report the de novo computational design of miniprotein binders targeting the leptin-binding site within the cytokine receptor homology 2 (CRH2) domain of LEPR. Computational screening and biochemical characterization identified the miniprotein binder Mini-19484, which adopted a stable -helical fold and exhibited enhanced resistance to proteolytic degradation. Mini-19484 bound the LEPR CRH2 domain with high affinity, with a dissociation constant (Kd) of 30 nM. Structural analysis of the predicted model and mutagenesis studies revealed that Arg18 of Mini-19484 serves as a critical interaction hotspot for LEPR binding. The predicted binding mode of Mini-19484 differed substantially from that of natural leptin, providing a distinct molecular scaffold for targeting the LEPR CRH2 domain. These findings provide a valuable framework for developing miniprotein-based therapeutics targeting LEPR.

papers.title: Wilson disease mechanisms manipulate ATP7B activity
papers.abstract: Copper is an essential cofactor for enzymes involved in diverse processes including mitochondrial respiration and the metabolism of neurotransmitters, collagen and melanin. However, its redox activity requires tight homeostatic control. The P-type ATPases ATP7A and ATP7B help deliver copper to cuproenzymes, and ATP7B mediates the excretion of excess copper into bile. Pathogenic ATP7B variants cause Wilson disease (WD), leading to copper accumulation in organs including the liver, kidney, and brain, and to disruption of copper-dependent processes. Current treatments primarily reduce systemic copper levels, while emerging gene therapies aim to restore ATP7B function. A complementary therapeutic strategy would be to rescue dysfunctional ATP7B using pharmacological chaperones, but their development is limited by an insufficient understanding of how WD variants perturb ATP7B structure and function. Here, we present a cryo-EM structure of human ATP7B reconstituted in lipid nanodiscs together with coarse-grained molecular dynamics simulations, as well as mutagenesis, functional and sequence analyses. We identify a salt bridge (E754-R969), crucial for the transition between inward- and outward-facing conformations, which is abolished by the R969Q disease variant. Additionally, we find a conserved stabilizing cholesterol-binding site severely disrupted by the WD variant W939C. Furthermore, we present new insights into the dynamics of metal binding domains 5 and 6 hinting at a copper relay mechanism in ATP7B. Together, these findings reveal lipid- and domain-mediated mechanisms of ATP7B regulation and explain how specific WD variants disrupt them, providing a structural framework for mutation-directed therapeutic strategies, including pharmacological chaperones.

papers.title: Visually guided analysis of single cell proteomics data with SCP-Viz
papers.abstract: Single cell proteomics (SCP) is a specialized, but expanding, field of research today. One of many challenges slowing SCP adoption is the inherent instability of the proteome and the changes that can occur before getting cells to a lab for preparation and analysis. Additionally, all current interpretation tools require experienced bioinformaticians to make the step from data to interpretation. Here, we present a visual toolkit that can accept SCP data from any instrument or common data processing algorithm. To demonstrate the capabilities of this tool we apply it to the analysis of dried digests of single human cancer cells following long room temperature storage. Remarkably, proteomic depth of the dried and stored samples analyzed is higher than the original analysis of these same digests on a similar system directly following isolation. Critically, when comparing control and drug treated cells, both the protein abundance and post-translationally modified peptides appear similar in both fresh and stored digests of these single cells. These findings are highly encouraging and, taken together, may help decrease the barriers for entry and collaboration for the field of SCP globally.

papers.title: Daphniphyllum macropodum genome assembly and multiplexed screening unveils alkaloid modifying enzymes
papers.abstract: Daphniphyllum macropodum, a small shrub or tree native to East Asia, produces bioactive polycyclic alkaloids of remarkable complexity and variety, making them long-standing, attractive targets for chemical synthesis. However, the biosynthetic origins of Daphniphyllum alkaloids remain unknown, and no pathway-associated enzymes have been identified to date. Here, we report the chromosome-level genome assembly of D. macropodum, representing the first genome assembly for the Daphniphyllaceae, a family in the Saxifragales woody clade. To discover alkaloid-modifying enzymes, we developed a highly combinatorial, multiplexed screening approach which enabled testing multiple enzyme candidates with multiple substrates in a single reaction. Deconvolution and characterisation identified two cytochrome P450 enzymes that catalyse the hydroxylation of the yuzurimine-type alkaloid daphhimalenine B. Specifically, CYP82C230 functions as a daphhimalenine B 2-hydroxylase to yield the natural product yuzurimine C, whereas its paralog, CYP82C231, acts as a daphhimalenine B 13-hydroxylase generating a novel alkaloid we have named yuzurimine F. These are the first reports of an enzymatic modification of a Daphniphyllum alkaloid. Collectively, this work advances our understanding of D. macropodum biology and represents the first steps towards elucidating the complex Daphniphyllum alkaloid biosynthetic pathway.

papers.title: Coordinated remodeling of NAD⁺ metabolic networks across the lifespan of Caenorhabditis elegans
papers.abstract: Changes in the metabolic network that sustain NAD+ during aging remain poorly understood. Analysis of steady state levels is insufficient to reveal whether biosynthetic or consumption pathways are perturbed or preserved. Here, we address this gap in understanding by integrating metabolomics, proteomics, gene-expression profiling, and stable-isotope tracing across the Caenorhabditis elegans adult lifespan. NAD abundance increases with age despite reductions in selected biosynthetic components. Tracing reveals reduced mid-adult incorporation of nicotinamide and nicotinic acid into NAD, alongside declining nicotinamide riboside abundance and loss of detectable nicotinic acid-derived labeling into this precursor. Early mitochondrial Complex I remodeling accompanies sustained changes in redox and energetic indices. Disruption of NAD-consuming or salvage enzymes reduces reproduction and lifespan, whereas precursor supplementation provides no longevity benefit under the conditions tested. Together, these findings reveal that NAD accumulation can coexist with extensive metabolic remodeling, establishing the importance of evaluating network dynamics beyond cofactor abundance.

papers.title: The crystal structure of the human SIPA1L2 PDZ domain reveals an atypically short, metazoan-conserved β2 β3 loop
papers.abstract: Signal - induced proliferation-associated 1-like protein 2 (SIPA1L2) is a large neuronal Rap GTPase-activating protein implicated in dynein-dependent retrograde transport of BDNF-TrkB signaling endosomes and genetically linked to Parkinson's disease. It consists of a RapGAP domain, a PDZ domain, and a coiled-coil domain separated by intrinsically disordered regions. Its compact PDZ domain mediates protein-protein interaction by binding short PDZ-binding motifs (PBM) in target proteins. Here, the human SIPA1L2 PDZ domain (residues 943-1027) was crystallized and its structure determined by molecular replacement. The domain adopts the canonical PDZ fold of six beta-strands forming two antiparallel beta-sheets flanked by two alpha-helices. The beta 2 - beta 3 loop, located next to the PBM binding groove, is unusually short - eight residues, against a 14-residue human-PDZome consensus. A BLASTP- and AlphaFold3-based survey across Metazoa shows that, despite PDZ sequence identities falling to ~25 %, the fold and the short loop are structurally conserved (Calpha; RMSD 0.5 - 0.8 Angstrom), indicating that this is a genuine, evolutionarily constrained architectural feature of SIPA1L2-type PDZ domains. PBM binding was not observed in co-crystallization trials. Native holdup assays against a neuronal proteome identified no specific partners for the SIPA1L2 PDZ domain. The structure retains the canonical carboxylate-binding loop and a class-I-type histidine, so partner scarcity is not due to loss of the PBM binding apparatus. Impaired PBM binding seems to result from the combination of the unusually short beta 2 - beta 3 loop and an evolutionarily invariant His964 located at the beta 2 strand. The short loop might restrict the conformational dynamics of the beta 2 strand, thereby stabilizing His964 side-chain conformations that encroach on the PBM binding groove. The structure thus defines SIPA1L2 as a structurally canonical yet apparently orphan PDZ domain.

papers.title: Cryo-EM structure of plant ABCC1 reveals mode of arsenic transport
papers.abstract: Plant ATP-binding cassette transporter C1 (ABCC1) mediates the vacuolar sequestration of heavy metal-phytochelatin (PC) complexes for cytosolic detoxification, yet the structural mechanisms of substrate recognition and metal coordination remain uncharacterized. Here, we report functional assays and single-particle cryo-EM structures of maize ABCC1 (ZmABCC1) in its apo state and bound to an PC2-As(III) complex. Functional assays demonstrate that ZmABCC1 ATPase activity is sequentially increased by glutathione, PC2, and PC3 in the presence of , supporting that longer PC chain lengths increase transport efficiency. The substrate-bound structure reveals the mode of substrate binding of the heavy metal complex, with the As(III) atom coordinated in a trigonal pyramidal geometry by three sulfur atoms from two PC2 ligands. Arg1200 plays a key role through nonpolar interaction with As(III) through its aliphatic side chain and an electrostatic interaction with the carboxyl group of PC2. These results define the molecular basis of PC-mediated heavy metal transport by plant ABCC1 which could be utilized to inform efforts to engineer crop stress resilience.

papers.title: FluoMALDI Imaging: An Integrated Multimodality Platform for Biologically Informed Spatial-Omics
papers.abstract: FluoMALDI imaging integrates fluorescence microscopy and matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization mass spectrometry imaging (MALDI-MSI) of tissues and cells, leveraging matrix-enhanced fluorescence signals to enable spatially guided functional molecular discovery. Here we report three broadly applicable FluoMALDI paradigms that link how genes, proteins, and organelles shape spatial molecular composition. These advances are achieved by integrating immuno-, HaloTag-, and dye-based labels into a unified FluoMALDI imaging framework. These approaches enabled us to interrogate cell-specific lipidomic compositions in human hippocampal vasculature, neural crest cells in chick embryo tissue, and human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived astrocytes. We also determined that fluorophore-MALDI matrix co-crystals resulted in FluoMALDI-induced fluorescence enhancements. Single-crystal X-ray crystallography showed that their co-crystallization produced localized, finite {pi}-{pi} interactions between two fluorophore molecules, or a fluorophore and a matrix molecule, throughout the crystal lattice. Together, these findings provide structural insight into the basis of fluorescence enhancement and support FluoMALDI as a broadly applicable multimodality imaging platform for biologically informed, cell-specific spatial-omics.

papers.title: Antibody full-length light chain reshapes variable domains aggregation without altering their dominance in amyloid fibrils
papers.abstract: AL amyloidosis is a fatal systemic amyloid disease in which antibody light chains (LCs), including full-length (FL) and their proteolytically fragmented variable (VL) and constant (CL) domains, aggregate within a complex extracellular matrix (ECM) across multiple tissues. However, how these co-existing species shape aggregation kinetics, fibril morphology, stability, and toxicity remains unexplored. In this work, using a patient-derived LC (AL55), we show that FL transiently interacts with VL, slowing its aggregation nearly four-fold and diverting it into protease-sensitive, seeding-incompetent protofibrillar aggregates rather than mature amyloid assemblies. VL alone or in the presence of inert CL instead matures into toxic, protease-resistant, seeding-competent helical fibrils. Owing to their greater protease resistance and seeding competence, VL-dominated amyloid assemblies persist and contribute to their enrichment within tissues. The FL-mediated redirection is generic across multiple amyloidogenic VLs. These results reveal that LC aggregation, like that of A{beta} and Tau, is governed by interplay between full-length and fragmented species, rather than VL domain aggregation in isolation. Overall, this work identifies a molecular basis for the selective enrichment of VL fibrils in patients and provides a therapeutic rationale for stabilizing VL domains to prevent their pathological aggregation.

papers.title: Rational Design of Molecular Glue Degraders Utilizing Endogenous Transient Protein-Protein Interactions
papers.abstract: Molecular glues are small molecules that modulate protein activity by inducing or stabilizing protein-protein interactions (PPIs). However, identifying and harnessing endogenous protein pairs amenable to small-molecule-mediated stabilization remains a major challenge in molecular glue development. Here we introduce transient interface pocket-guided molecular glue rational design (TrIP-MGRD), a strategy that shifts compound discovery from empirical screening toward rational, interaction-guided design by exploiting druggable pockets at transient PPI interfaces. Using CDK12 as a model target, we identified DDB1 as an endogenous transient interaction partner and determined the DDB1-CDK12-CCNK complex structure by cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). Structure-guided virtual screening and medicinal chemistry optimization yielded a molecular glue C432 that stabilized this interaction. Comparison of the ligand-free and C432-bound complexes revealed pre-existing contacts at the transient CDK12-DDB1 interface provides a structural basis for compound-mediated stabilization. Collectively, by integrating endogenous partner identification with interface-guided screening, TrIP-MGRD provides a new framework for target-directed molecular glue discovery.

papers.title: Gut Microbial Butyrate Metabolism Generates an N-Acyl Amide that Regulates Host Transcriptional Programs
papers.abstract: Faecalibacterium prausnitzii is a prominent member of the human gut microbiota whose depletion is associated with various intestinal and metabolic disorders. While multiple mechanisms have been proposed to explain how F. prausnitzii promotes host health, the molecular determinants underlying these activities remain elusive. Here, we show that F. prausnitzii is a prolific producer of the human metabolite N-butyrylglycine, which we find accumulates to millimolar concentrations in bacterial culture and is readily detectable in the feces of conventional wildtype mice. We establish an enzymatic basis of N-butyrylglycine production by identifying and biochemically validating an F. prausnitzii N-acyltransferase that catalyzes the conjugation of butyryl-CoA and glycine. Despite being derived from butyrate, N-butyrylglycine exhibits distinct bioactivity from its precursor, including reduced histone deacetylase inhibitory activity, an altered inflammatory profile, and enhanced suppression of cellular proliferation across multiple cancer cell lines. Furthermore, transcriptomic profiling revealed N butyrylglycine coordinates repression of G2/M checkpoint-associated programs and downregulation of the colorectal cancer associated gene AOC1. Together, these findings suggest that specialized metabolites produced by F. prausnitzii contribute to its beneficial effects and may underlie its protective role in colorectal cancer.

papers.title: How a Disease-Associated Mutation Destabilizes the Sliding Clamp PCNA
papers.abstract: The eukaryotic sliding clamp, Proliferating Cell Nuclear Antigen (PCNA), is a homo-trimeric ring-shaped protein complex that encircles DNA and serves as a scaffold for enzymes during DNA replication and the DNA damage response. Patients harboring the homozygous point mutation C148S in PCNA have the genetic disease PCNA Associated DNA Repair Disorder (PARD). Our lab showed that this PCNA variant has a drastic 10 {degrees}C thermostability defect. However, the crystal structure of the C148S variant displays a nearly identical conformation as WT PCNA, so it remained unclear how this point mutation destabilizes PCNA. Here, we use extensive all-atom classical molecular dynamics and well-tempered metadynamics simulations to predict how this mutation destabilizes PCNA. We first show that the C148S substitution changes an internal hydrogen-bond network and permits water molecules to transiently bind within the protein core, distorting the -helix containing C148S. This distortion in turn weakens the subunit interface, providing a molecular explanation for the lowered stability of the PCNA ring. Thus, our study addresses the molecular mechanism by which this disease-associated variant destabilizes PCNA and highlights the importance of understanding protein dynamics to interpret the effects of mutations in disease.

papers.title: MolMap resolves functional chromatin responses to small-molecule perturbation
papers.abstract: Small molecules can alter chromatin through protein-, DNA- and physicochemical interactions, yet current approaches do not directly resolve where these perturbations produce an immediate functional chromatin response in native nuclear environments. Here we present MolMap (chromatin-small Molecule Mapping), a sequencing-based method that profiles genome-wide chromatin responses to chemically unmodified compounds in isolated, non-crosslinked nuclei. Rather than measuring ligand binding, protein occupancy or downstream gene expression, MolMap identifies genomic regions where small-molecule exposure produces an immediate functional chromatin response. By quantifying changes in Tn5 accessibility and local chromatin organization in native nuclei, MolMap captures locus-specific and dose-dependent effects while separating early chromatin responses from downstream cellular adaptation. Across metabolites, protein-targeting compounds, a DNA-binding drug and a physicochemical chromatin modulator, MolMap resolved compound-specific and mechanistically distinct responses. Comparison with live-cell ATAC-seq showed that MolMap captures early chromatin responses before broader cellular adaptation. In leukemia models, MolMap revealed a coordinated chromatin response in drug-sensitive cells that was strongly attenuated in resistant models. MolMap therefore provides a native framework for bridging the precision of biochemical perturbation assays with the breadth of genome-wide profiling, extending classical chromatin biochemistry into a genomic setting.

papers.title: A Molecular Glue that Regulates Processing of Non-Coding RNAs in Human Cells
papers.abstract: Small nuclear RNAs (snRNAs) are a major class of non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) and essential components of the spliceosome. Chemical tools for perturbing snRNA structure and function are lacking, and ncRNAs have more generally been considered undruggable. Here we use chemical proteomics and cryo-electron microscopy to identify a covalent molecular glue HL-1B that stabilizes binding of the 3'-exonuclease TOE1 to the spliceosome in a catalytically competent state. We show that HL-1B triggers excess 3'-processing of snRNAs in human cells that is tunable by the expression levels of TOE1 and auxiliary splicing regulators like SNRPB2, which, in turn, create synthetic lethality interactions with HL-1B that correlate with the preferential modulation of intermediate exon inclusion splicing events. Our findings reveal a fundamental role for snRNA tail length in regulating spliceosome function and, more generally, a way to target ncRNAs with non-orthosteric small molecules that remodel the interactomes of RNA processing enzymes in cells.

papers.title: IMPRESS: AI-coupled HPC workflows for protein design
papers.abstract: Protein design campaigns are often run as multi-stage pipelines with a generative backbone model, an inverse-folding model, and a structure predictor chained together in that order. The stages differ by one to two orders of magnitude in cost per candidate, and the allocation of sampling effort across them is fixed before a campaign begins. Such a filter cascade can only discard candidates. It cannot redirect sampling toward the regions of design space a model stack can reach, and for targets whose constraints are far from the generative model's training distribution it may return no solution at any practical sample count. We present IMPRESS (Integrated Machine-learning for PRotein Structures at Scale), a framework in which design pipelines are stateful objects that halt, continue, resample, or branch at runtime from their own accumulated results. Adaptive decisions are evaluated asynchronously with respect to execution, so a campaign refines itself without global synchronization. We apply IMPRESS to three problems: backbone generation on discontinuous enzyme active-site motifs, de novo small molecule binder design, and PDZ binder redesign. Adaptive parameterization solves active-site motifs carried on three or more discontinuous residue islands that a fixed cascade does not solve, shifts the realized task mix toward inexpensive sequence exploration, and produces sequence ensembles that explore broadly but stay near their inputs. All comparisons reported here are between in silico metrics. We expect that adaptive parameterization will matter most for targets furthest from the training distributions of the underlying models, and that the same primitives will accommodate experimental measurement as a steering signal.

papers.title: Tetrapeptide caspase inhibitors exhibit protease- and substrate-dependent off-target specificity
papers.abstract: Peptide-based caspase inhibitors are widely used to define the functions of individual caspases and were developed from tetrapeptide substrate preferences identified using positional scanning peptide libraries. Their specificity is typically validated using fluorogenic tetrapeptide substrates, yet whether these assays accurately predict inhibition of endogenous protein substrates has not been systematically examined. Here, we demonstrate that the widely used executioner caspase inhibitor zDEVD-FMK directly inhibits caspase-1 (CASP1)-mediated processing of interleukin-1{beta} (IL-1{beta}) and interleukin-18 (IL-18) despite CASP1 exhibiting minimal activity toward the DEVD fluorogenic substrate. Unexpectedly, zDEVD-FMK selectively inhibited CASP1 but not the closely related inflammatory caspases CASP4 or CASP5. Conversely, the CASP1 inhibitor Ac-YVAD-CMK directly inhibited CASP3-mediated protein substrate cleavage. We further found that endogenous substrates displayed markedly different sensitivities to inhibition, with IL-1{beta} and IL-18 processing consistently inhibited more efficiently than gasdermin D cleavage, while fluorogenic CASP3/7 reporter cleavage substantially overestimated inhibition of endogenous apoptotic substrates. During inflammasome activation and Salmonella infection, DEVD- and YVAD-based inhibitors failed to distinguish apoptotic executioner caspase activity from inflammatory caspase signaling. Together, our findings demonstrate that fluorogenic tetrapeptide assays do not faithfully predict inhibition of endogenous protein substrates and identify protease- and substrate-dependent specificity as fundamental features of peptide-based caspase inhibitors.

papers.title: SMSTPred: Protein Language Model Embeddings Predict SAM-Methyltransferase Substrate Specificity and Reveal Metabolite Methyltransferasome Enrichment in Plants and Actinomycetota
papers.abstract: S-adenosyl-methionine (SAM)-dependent methyltransferases (MTases) are one of the largest and most ancient enzyme superfamilies in biology, transferring a methyl group from SAM to substrates as different as DNA, RNA, proteins, and small-molecule metabolites. Most SAM-MTases share a Class I Rossmann-like SAM-binding core, with substrate specificity determined by variable inserts and accessory domains rather than the conserved fold; as a result, substrate type is unknown for most MTases in sequence databases, which are dominated by unreviewed entries. Here we present SMSTPred (SAM-Methyltransferase Substrate-Type Predictor), a multi-label classifier that predicts MTase substrate type from protein language model embeddings and benchmarks it under homology-disjoint cross-validation against sequence-homology, structure-homology, and profile-HMM baselines. SMSTPred reaches a cluster-disjoint Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.94, significantly ahead of sequence-homology (MMseqs2, 0.85), structure-homology (Foldseek, 0.89) and profile-HMM (0.52) baselines, while providing calibrated, per-substrate confidence. Applying it to ~116,000 MTases across 1,249 reference proteomes, we map the substrate landscape of methylation across the tree of life. Substrate specialization tracks taxonomy: animals expand protein- and DNA-methylation, whereas small-molecule methyltransferases are enriched in plants and Actinomycetota; in Actinomycetota beyond what is expected for their proteome size, and in plants in proportion to their larger proteomes. The predictions identify thousands of uncharacterized methyltransferases with substrate type assignments (about half of those in uncharacterized clusters), many corroborated by an independent reaction-retrieval method. Notably, ~11% of enzymes with a single substrate call lack any class-discriminative sequence motif, suggesting that substrate specificity is often encoded beyond short linear motifs. Together, this work provides SMSTPred, a substrate-type predictor for Class I methyltransferases, and a tree-of-life resource of testable functional hypotheses.

papers.title: Biosynthesis of serotonergic Kanna alkaloids
papers.abstract: Plants have repeatedly evolved to synthesize natural products that exploit serotonin signaling in animals. Although serotonin and most of its neuroactive analogs derive from tryptophan, the medicinal Kanna plant (Mesembryanthemum tortuosum) instead uses tyrosine and phenylalanine to construct a serotonin-like scaffold through unknown chemical transformations. Here, we elucidate the biosynthesis of Kanna alkaloids, including the serotonin reuptake inhibitor mesembrine. We reveal an unusual scaffold-forming strategy that is mediated by non-canonical transferase and oxidase enzymes, and we provide mechanistic insight on how an activated biosynthetic intermediate undergoes a multistep cyclization cascade to form the Kanna alkaloid scaffold. Collectively, our work uncovers how plants repurpose unconventional metabolic building blocks and enzymes to produce serotonergic molecules with promise as therapeutics for neurological disorders.

papers.title: Repurposing a biosynthetic enzyme for imaging UDP-glucose dynamics in living systems
papers.abstract: Metabolite dynamics remain difficult to visualize in living systems, particularly for nucleotide sugars that link metabolism to glycosylation and signaling. Here we repurpose Helicobacter pylori UDP-glucose pyrophosphorylase to develop UGluS, a genetically encoded ratiometric fluorescent sensor for its biosynthetic product, UDP-glucose (UDP-Glc). Circularly permuted GFP insertion and directed evolution yield an approximately 18-fold excitation-ratio response and an apparent dissociation constant of 32.5 M, with preferential responsiveness to UDP-Glc over related metabolites. Live-cell imaging and microplate assays reveal responses to metabolic, genetic and mechanosensitive perturbations in mammalian cells. In zebrafish larvae, UGluS reveals uridine-induced increases in UDP-Glc availability and fin-fold enrichment. In mouse liver slices and skeletal muscle in vivo, insulin- and glucose-induced decreases in UDP-Glc availability accompany increased glycogen content. These findings establish UGluS as a tool for imaging UDP-Glc dynamics across biological scales and extend the use of biosynthetic enzymes as fluorescent sensing scaffolds.

papers.title: De Novo Design of C-H Hydroxylation Enzymes with Programmed Selectivities
papers.abstract: The ability to precisely functionalize individual C-H bonds in complex organic molecules would transform synthetic strategies to produce essential chemicals. In nature, C-H oxidations are commonly achieved using metalloenzymes such as cytochrome P450s, however adapting these systems to achieve selective conversions of complex substrates requires extensive enzyme discovery and engineering campaigns. Here we show that selective C-H oxidation biocatalysts can be programmed computationally from minimal structural inputs comprising a Cys-ligated heme cofactor, catalytic side chains required for H2O2 activation and heterolysis, and the target substrate precisely positioned adjacent to the resulting ferryl intermediate (Compound I). We designed heme hydroxylases for increasingly complex substrates, progressing from aromatic and aliphatic oxidations of fluorogenic model compounds to regiodivergent oxidation of estradiol at either the benzylic C6 (93% d.e.) or unactivated C16 (99% d.e.) positions. Crystal structures across all campaigns confirm the accuracy of the design pipeline. Together, these results establish a general framework for constructing selective heme hydroxylases around predefined substrates and reaction geometries, providing a path toward custom biocatalysts for site-selective C-H functionalizations.

papers.title: Genome-Guided Discovery and Biosynthetic Characterization of Burkstatins, Bicyclic Microviridins with Protease Inhibitory Activity
papers.abstract: Microviridins are ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides characterized by a highly constrained macrocyclic scaffold and potent serine protease inhibitory activity. Unlike canonical tricyclic microviridins, bicyclic microviridins, exemplified by marinostatins, lack the characteristic {omega}-amide linkage. The biosynthetic diversity and biological activities of bicyclic microviridins remain poorly explored. Here, genome mining and phylogenetic analyses revealed diverse lineages of putative bicyclic microviridins, including a conserved family of multicore precursors in Burkholderiaceae. We characterized a representative biosynthetic gene cluster from Paraburkholderia sp. CNPSo 3076 and demonstrated that a single ATP-grasp ligase, BksD, catalyzes the formation of two {omega}-ester macrocycles within each of the two precursor core regions. Heterologous reconstitution and tandem mass spectrometric analyses enabled the production and structural characterization of two bicyclic peptides, designated burkstatin 1 and burkstatin 2. Despite sharing a conserved bicyclic scaffold, the two peptides exhibited distinct serine protease inhibitory profiles. Burkstatin 2 potently inhibited subtilisin and elastase, whereas burkstatin 1 displayed weaker subtilisin inhibition and no detectable elastase inhibition. These findings expand the known biosynthetic and functional diversity of bicyclic microviridins, demonstrate the capacity of a single ATP-grasp ligase to modify multiple core peptides and highlight the influence of core sequence variation on protease inhibitory activity.

papers.title: Trapping more seeing more, benchmarking a new trap column for low-input proteomics
papers.abstract: Nanoflow liquid chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry (LC-MS) has become central to low-input and single-cell proteomics (SCP), where trap-and-elute workflows offer sample loading flexibility and analytical column protection but introduce additional dead volume, surface area, and a largely uncharacterized trade-off between flush direction and chromatographic performance. Here, we present a systematic, iterative benchmarking study of a purpose-built family of NanoShield trap columns against the established PepMap Neo trap cartridge and direct injection. Using a standardized workflow built on a commercial HeLa digest standard, we evaluated performance across two mass spectrometry platforms, multiple LC gradient lengths, both flush directions, and a range of sample input amounts and injection volumes. Shortening of the NanoShield packed bed, from an initial 5 cm format to a 1.2 cm format, closed a substantial sample loading time penalty and largely eliminated a pronounced forward-flush performance deficit, while remaining superior to the PepMap in reverse-flush mode and approaching direct injection level identification numbers, peak width, and quantitative precision. A next-generation NanoShield featuring a stationary phase with larger pore size further narrowed the residual forward-flush penalty. These results demonstrate that trap column bed length and stationary phase chemistry are key, partially independent design levers for closing the performance gap between trap-and-elute and direct injection workflows, and provide practical, present-day guidance for trap column selection and operation in low-input proteomics.

papers.title: Structural basis of SBDS dysfunction in Shwachman-Diamond Syndrome
papers.abstract: Surveillance of functional centers in the mature 60S ribosomal subunit by SBDS licenses its translational debut. Timely release of eIF6 from 60S by SBDS is essential to permit 40S joining. Biallelic mutations in SBDS associated with Shwachman-Diamond syndrome (SDS), an inherited ribosomopathy, impair dissociation of eIF6 from 60S. How SBDS variants that bind to 60S structurally perturb the maturation and surveillance of 60S is yet to be deciphered. Here, we report high-resolution cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) structures of human SBDS and pathogenic variants in complex with human 60S. The structures reveal that disease mutations disrupt key interactions of SBDS with the functional centers of the 60S subunit destabilizing critical bases and protein interactions across the P-site, peptidyl transferase center, polypeptide exit tunnel and GTPase-associated center. These mutations remodel the N-terminal contacts with 60S, altering critical interactions with uL16 (RPL10) distant from the mutation site. Mutations in domains II and III trigger conformational changes that propagate across the entirety of SBDS and remodel distant ribosomal regions, revealing an elegant mechanism of pathogenic allostery. The profound effects of SBDS mutations on both the surveillance and mature conformation of the 60S subunit provide a structural framework for understanding the molecular pathology of SDS.

papers.title: De novo design of antiviral monobody binders
papers.abstract: Monobodies (Mobs) are a class of immunoglobulin (Ig)-like proteins that have emerged as promising therapeutic scaffolds for applications ranging from antiviral therapy to cancer treatment. Unlike conventional monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), Mobs can be readily expressed in Escherichia coli at high yields, offering important advantages in overall developability. However, discovering antigen-specific Mobs with high binding affinity traditionally requires screening large, randomized in vitro libraries. To optimize Mob discovery, we developed MobGen, a computational pipeline for de novo design of Mob binders against viral antigens. As a proof of concept, we generated Mobs that bind the SARS-CoV-2 Spike glycoprotein Receptor Binding Domain (RBD). Subsequent in silico optimization improved production yield, thermal and conformational stability, binding affinity, and antiviral activity, demonstrating a promising approach for rapidly developing antibody-like molecules that target viral entry. These findings highlight MobGen's potential for de novo design of Mobs against emerging viruses with pandemic potential.

papers.title: Discovery of cell-permeable inhibitors for human succinyl-CoA:glutarate-CoA transferase
papers.abstract: Glutaric Aciduria Type I (GA-1) is a recessive, serious neurometabolic disorder characterized by a build-up of toxic metabolites in the lysine metabolic pathway with no current pharmacological treatment. Previous mouse studies have shown that a deficiency in SUGCT attenuates the accumulation of some of these metabolites in vivo. These results highlight the potential for SUGCT as a therapeutic target in treating GA-1. We had previously identified biochemical inhibitors for SUGCT and had solved the crystal structure of the protein, both apo and bound to an inhibitor. However, we were unable to demonstrate cellular activity for these compounds. In this study, we report findings from additional in vitro high-throughput screening and address these challenges by developing an improved cell-based assay to detect SUGCT inhibition. We show that by improving the permeability of valsartan using its ethyl ester prodrug, SUGCT is effectively inhibited in GA-1 cells. We also identify meclofenamic acid as a new SUGCT inhibitor with cellular activity, providing additional validation and highlighting this enzyme target potential for GA-1.

papers.title: Deep sequence-function mapping reveals computationally unpredictable epistatic trajectories that drive laboratory evolution
papers.abstract: The black-box nature of directed evolution has been constraining advances in enzyme engineering and the wider application of engineered biocatalysts. While conventional deep sequence-function mapping has delivered insights into sequence space architecture, it lacks the ability to analyse adaptive landscapes and fully grasp the long-term impact of epistasis on the accessibility of evolutionary trajectories. Here, we introduce Deep Evolutionary Trajectory Mapping (dETM) which tracks the winners of a multi-round evolutionary campaign to map catalytic rates across the adaptive landscape of an imine reductase. We identified founder variants as stepping stones towards fitness peaks and recognise positive epistasis as their competitive advantage over alternative lineages. State-of-the-art machine learning models could not predict the resulting winning trajectories, which highlights the importance of decoding design principles for successful evolution experimentally. Permissive selection and ultrahigh-throughput screening emerge as foundations of derisking landscape traversal by keeping multiple paths accessible and avoiding diminishing returns.
